title: He set his face (Luke 9:51–62)
hookLine: he turns toward Jerusalem; foxes have holes, but he has nowhere to lay his head

cards: Halfway through chapter nine, Luke's Gospel turns a corner, and you can almost feel the road tilt.
In the King James words: "when the time was come that he should be received up, he stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem." From here on, Jesus is walking.
The Good Samaritan, the prodigal son, Zacchaeus in the tree: Luke sets them on the road to Jerusalem, where Jesus has already said what is waiting.
Some readers hear an echo of Isaiah, where God's servant says: "therefore have I set my face like a flint." Flint. Hard stone.

teach.b: The road goes through Samaria first. In John's Gospel, a Samaritan woman names one old dispute between Samaritans and Jews: where to worship.
Jesus sends messengers ahead to find a place to stay, and a Samaritan village turns them away, Luke says, because he was heading to Jerusalem.

teach.h: FIRE FROM HEAVEN? HE REBUKED THEM.
teach.b: James and John are furious: "Lord, wilt thou that we command fire to come down from heaven, and consume them, even as Elias did?" And Luke says: "he turned, and rebuked them." They simply go to another village.
Then three people meet him on the road. The first says, I'll follow you anywhere.
Jesus: "Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head." Anywhere includes nowhere. To the second, Jesus says: follow me.

The man says, let me first go and bury my father. Jesus: "Let the dead bury their dead." Readers differ: some think the father had just died, others that the man meant to wait until his father died someday.
The text doesn't say. What's clear is the urgency. The third says, let me first say goodbye to my family.

teach.h: HAND TO THE PLOUGH, NO LOOKING BACK.
teach.b: And Jesus answers: "No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God."

teach.h: HE STEDFASTLY SET HIS FACE TO GO TO JERUSALEM.
teach.b: Look back over your shoulder and the furrow goes crooked. You keep your eyes on a point ahead, and walk toward it.

how: Commentators call this long stretch of Luke the travel narrative, and some Christians read through it slowly, a few verses a day, as a journey toward Jerusalem and Holy Week.

o: a hard stone, a picture of steady resolve
a stubborn refusal to listen to anyone
a spark that calls down fire from heaven

games.q: what's inside Luke 9:51–62 — tap the pairs.

s: Jesus called down fire on the Samaritan village
James and John wanted to; he turned and rebuked them.
from here, much of Luke happens on the road to Jerusalem
Luke sets the stories that follow on the road.
Luke explains exactly what "let the dead bury their dead" meant
the text doesn't say, and readers still differ.

games.q: a village refuses to welcome you. your two closest friends ask: shall we call down fire on them? what do you do?
o: turn and rebuke them, and go to another village.
send messengers to argue with the village.
games.why: he rebukes James and John, and they simply go on to another village.

practice: Bring to mind something you keep circling and not doing, a hard conversation, a doctor's appointment, an apology, and notice the let-me-first voices, the someday.
Picture a plowman with his eyes on the far side of the field, and your own face set toward that one thing, calm and steady, then choose the very first step.
If you pray, you can ask for a steady face; if you don't, simply fix your eyes on the step.

wordCard.voice: Flint, the hard stone Isaiah uses for an unbending resolve: Luke's turning point, where Jesus sets his face to go to Jerusalem and will not be turned back.

orig.note: Greek: he set firm his face. the King James Bible says stedfastly set his face.

carryVoice: Your line: no looking back. The furrow runs straight when your eyes stay ahead. Day five hundred thirty-eight.
